name: Nabataean Civilization 30BC - 106 AD
description: Before 170 BC, the Nabataeans functioned mainly as a loosely organized tribal confederation controlling caravan routes across southern Jordan and northern Arabia. Around 170 BC, the emergence of documented kings marks political centralization and territorial control. The kingdom flourished through trade until Rome peacefully annexed it in AD 106, absorbing it as the province of Arabia Petraea.

name: Kingdom of Cyprus 1192-1489 AD
description: The Kingdom of Cyprus was created in 1192 when Guy of Lusignan acquired the island after the Third Crusade, establishing a Crusader-style monarchy. Strategic for trade and military control, Cyprus gradually fell under Venetian influence. In 1489, political pressure led Queen Caterina Cornaro to cede the island to Venice, ending the kingdom.

name: Kingdom of Jerusalem 1099-1187 AD
description: The Kingdom of Jerusalem was founded in 1099 after the First Crusade, when crusaders captured the Holy City and established a Latin feudal monarchy in the Levant. Its survival depended on narrow supply routes, European support, and powerful military orders. Between 1186 and 1187, the crushing defeat at Hattin allowed Saladin to reconquer almost all its territory, including Jerusalem.

name: Kingdom of Jerusalem 1268-1291 AD
description: The Kingdom of Jerusalem slowly withered as the Mamluks cut down its coastal enclaves one by one. In 1291, Acre, the last great Crusader stronghold, fell after a desperate defense, its walls shattered and its defenders pushed into the sea. With Acre’s collapse, the Crusader kingdom vanished from the Middle East, ending nearly two centuries of Latin rule.

name: Achaemenid Empire 539–530 BC
description: Following Babylon's fall in 539 BC, Cyrus established a superpower spanning from the Indus to the Ionian coast. He governed Greek poleis through tribute and local tyrants while focusing his final years on securing the northeastern frontiers. Although Cyrus died in 530 BC, the Achaemenid dynasty he founded remained the world's dominant force until its final collapse in 330 BC.

name: Achaemenid Empire 513–480 BC
languages: Old Persian, Elamite, Babylonian, Aramaic (Lingua Franca)
description: In 513 BC, Darius I crossed the Danube, bringing Thrace and Macedonia under Persian control and establishing a transcontinental empire. For decades, the Satrapy system and Royal Road ensured stability from the Indus to Libya. However, 480 BC was a turning point. Following defeats at Salamis and Plataea, Xerxes I's invasion of Greece failed. The empire lost its European territories and Aegean hegemony to a Greek alliance led by Athens and Sparta, marking the beginning of its territorial retreat in the Mediterranean.

name: Imperial State of Iran 1971–1979
description: In 1970, Iran formally waived its claim to Bahrain, but in 1971 it strategically seized the islands of Abu Musa and the Tunbs, establishing its final maritime borders. Under the Shah, Iran became a dominant regional military power in the Persian Gulf. This period ended in 1979 when the Pahlavi dynasty was overthrown during the Islamic Revolution.

name: Islamic Republic of Iran 1979–Present
description: Established after the 1979 Revolution, this theocratic state maintained its 1971 borders despite the brutal Iran-Iraq War (1980–1988), which ended in a territorial status quo. Iran kept control of the strategic islands in the Strait of Hormuz. Today, it remains a central power in the Middle East, with its geographic limits unchanged since the diplomatic and military movements of the early 1970s.

name: Kingdom of Bahrain 1971–Present
description: Following the British withdrawal and Iran’s formal waiver of its territorial claims in 1970, Bahrain declared full independence on August 15, 1971. Led by the Al Khalifa dynasty, the island nation transitioned from a British protectorate to a sovereign state. Despite being a small archipelago, it became a major financial hub and strategic ally in the Gulf, maintaining its borders unchanged since its mid-20th-century diplomatic stabilization.

name: Kingdom of Saudi Arabia (2000–Present)
description: Established in 1932 after the unification of Nejd and Hejaz, the Kingdom finalized its modern shape through major border treaties. It dissolved Neutral Zones with Kuwait (1970) and Iraq (1981), dividing territories equally. The last significant change occurred in 2000 with the Treaty of Jeddah, which permanently settled the long-disputed southern frontier with Yemen, securing the nation’s current territorial integrity.

name: Qatar (2001–Present
description: Since its 1971 independence from British protection, Qatar has transformed from a pearl-diving economy into a global energy powerhouse. Under the Al Thani dynasty, it leveraged the world's largest gas fields to drive rapid modernization. In 2001 after a World Court ruling settled border disputes with Bahrain, allowing the peninsula to focus on its role as a key international mediator and cultural hub.

name: United Arab Emirates (1974–Present)
description: Formed in 1971 after the British withdrawal, the UAE is a unique federation of seven monarchies that transformed from desert sheikhdoms into a global hub of innovation and luxury. Led by Abu Dhabi and Dubai, the nation stabilized its borders through a 1974 treaty with Saudi Arabia. Today, it stands as a major financial power, famous for its visionary architecture and for successfully diversifying its economy beyond oil.
